text: We started with simple models running on GPUs.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Then we saw the evolution of model-serving frameworks like VLLM, DotServe, Triton.

text: And now we are watching the orchestration layer emerging in real time, addressing the complex challenges of routing, KV cache management, pre-field decode desegregation, and multi-model multiplexing.

text: So let's talk a little bit about agentic demand explosion.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: In the classical web serving before the AI inference workloads kicked off, the capacity scale roughly linearly with users, depending upon the workload type, double the users, mostly double the QPS, double the infrastructure fleet if there are no optimizations, and capacity planning was mostly a spreadsheet exercise.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: In this new agentic serving, capacity is scaling with number of users time, number of calls per users times number of tokens, which varies depending on the model, the optimizations, the hardware SKU you have.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: A chatbot can have one model call per turn,
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Which is evolving now with 10 to 20 for co-pilots and 50 for research agents.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: And now it's thousands of such calls for autonomous workloads with no human in the loop.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: The key takeaway that you cannot plan capacity for the agents the same way we did for microservices.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: We need to think about elasticity and implement workload-aware scheduling and admission control.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Now, let's try to dive a little bit deep into the differences, pros and cons, differences between the traditional microservice serving versus the modern inference serving across these key dimensions.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: The request shape.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Microservices assume short, uniform request, wherever the LLM requests we are seeing in our workloads, they can vary from 50 tokens to 100,000 tokens, with vastly different compute profiles between pre-fill and decode stage.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: For batching, classical stacks for microservices was doing stacking, batching mostly at the load balance layer, if at all.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: However, LLM serving requires continuous in-flight batching, how otherwise the throughput collapses by an order of magnitude or more.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: State, most of the classical microservices were stateless when we're not talking about storage layer.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: However, LLM serving does require a huge per request state, the KVCache, which is very expensive to build and even more expensive to throw away.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Scaling units.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: When we think about traditional microservices, we could run them in cheap CPUs, in pods.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: However, for modern inferencing, we're required to run on GPUs, which are 100 times more expensive, which are 10 times slower to acquire, and we cannot over-provision them casually.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Otherwise, it will lead to a huge wastage.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Failure mode.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: When you think about traditional microservices like most of us have built over the last couple of years, we could, even if a host crashed or a pod crashed, we could restart it.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: We could rebuild the state if needed be.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: However, for the model inferencing, it takes a huge amount of time to go from cold to hot startup.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: And these, and if a GPU is mid-decode, it can drop thousands of in-flight tokens and it can lead to a queue buildup.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: The takeaway is that the bottleneck is not just the model, it's the orchestration itself.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: As we can see in these hidden decisions behind a prompt, when we go to any genetic application, it requires a bunch of steps which are behind the scenes.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: We have to authenticate.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: We have to choose a model depending on the request type.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: We have to select the region where it goes.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: We have to do admission control.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: We have to do caching lookup.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: We have to run it on the GPU.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: We have to do batching.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: And there's a bunch of other steps involved.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: And as we can see, out of all these steps, only one step requires the model, which is the prefilled decode, if it's disaggregated inference or just if it's not disaggregated inference.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Other steps require infrastructure.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: The intelligence might lie in the model, but the economics, the reliability, and the user experience are all in the infrastructure.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: And this is why a lot of platform teams across a lot of companies are having much more impact on the product quality and the success much more than before.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Most of us in this room have a deep expertise across one or two or three layers.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: We might own kernels or kernel optimizations.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: We might own routing or the product itself, or we might be operating the GPU infrastructure or the cluster itself.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: But very few of us have operated the whole stack or thought about it end to end.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: As you can see in these layers, these layers are not new.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: They have been around for 20 years or more.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: What is new is the combination and the coupling between them.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: A decision at the routing layer can change the cache hit rate at the model layer, which can change the batch composition, which can change the GPU utilization, which can change the auto-scaling decision because of the change in GPU utilization.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So, everything is entangled.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: When we have any regressions in our inference workloads, it's not just about understanding what happened at the caching layer or admission control.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: We need to think about the stack top to bottom.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: And when we see any bottleneck, it's very, very important to understand at which layer is that bottleneck so that we can invest properly.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Now diving a little bit deep into how a prompt works.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: When we have a prompt for any application, be it just if you want to generate an image, or if you have a research task, or if you have complex multi-agent orchestration, more or less, it involves a bunch of these steps.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: The prompt goes to the gateway.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Then it goes to the router, after which it does the cache lookup if the request was already seen before.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Then it goes to the schedulers, which decides on which GPU cluster it should run, and on which hardware.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: It can be on NVIDIA or AMD or your in-house silicon chip, which then goes to the appropriate serving runtime, VLL, MSGLang, or whatever we are working on.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: And then we extreme the response back to the user according to the SLO profiles of time to first token and time between each token, and while making sure the throughput is what the user desired.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Now, as we can see, this inference behaves like a distributed transaction.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Each arrow in this diagram is a network hop.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Every one of these hops can retry.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: It can time out.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: It can fall back.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: It can even fail.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: And each of these hops will have an SLOs, and it is streaming back to the user.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So, if it fails, the partial philisemantics are much harder to deal with than for a regular RPC call.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Think about what happens if we have already streamed 200 tokens back to the user and suddenly a GPU host is preempted due to a scheduled or a planned or unplanned maintenance event.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: We cannot just retry.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: We have to think about it holistically.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: This is why reliability, we cannot build reliability at the edge.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: It has to be a property of the control plane because the control plane is the one which sees the whole workflow.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Now let's talk about schedulers and some of the optimizations and how we can think about it.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So for the traditional microservices, we used to think about bin packing of traditional microservices across three, four dimensions.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Could be across the socialization, CPU memory, or could be across four domains, depending upon if you're using AWS, if you're using your own in-house cloud providers.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: But for inference, the scheduler needs to be aware of across at least seven access when we schedule a particular request.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: It has to be aware of the GPU type.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: There can be any number of heterogeneous hardwares in your cluster, H100 versus E100 versus B200, with different network topologies.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: It has to be aware of the HPM headroom, KV cache state.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: The model waits whether they're already loaded, whether they're cold or we have to, whether they've already warmed up, we have to cold start it.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: It has to be aware of the tenant priority.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: There can be any number of tenants running on that multi-tenant cluster with different SLO profiles.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: We have to also be aware of the workflow context.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Are we in the third step of reasoning that has already spent X dollar or are we at the initial stages and we can terminate the workflow if we are over-provisioned?
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: We have to also think about latency budget, depending upon the type of agentic application we are building.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So this brings us to the idea that we have to make sure that we implement agentic aware scheduling.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: We have to make sure that we have placed the work which will finish in the fastest and the cheapest time, as opposed to just placing it on a random GPU.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: A concrete example might be that the skiller needs to be aware that request R is at step three of a five-minute workflow, and step one and two has already spent X plus Y dollar.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So if a step three fails, the whole workflow will be terminated, and we have wasted all that compute resources.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: That's why workflow-aware orchestration is very, very important because it will change the admission decisions, the priority, and how we retry.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Now let's talk about optimizations.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: I will not go too deep into a lot of optimizations.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: There's a lot of research which has already been done outside, but I would like to share a framework which at least I like to use when it comes to it.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: And we can place it into four quadrants.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: First, can we avoid the work?
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Meaning, can we skip it entirely through caching?
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Through techniques like prefix caching, response caching, semantic caching.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: The second, can we share the work?
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Can multiple requests share compute through batching?
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Think content batching, pre-fail decode, chunk pre-fail, specular decoding.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Third, can we move away the work?
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Can we send it somewhere to a cheaper model or closer to the user through mostly routing?
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Can we route it to a smaller model or a cheaper region or some other techniques?
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: And lastly, can we delay the work?
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Can we wait for a better moment through admission control and queuing, which requires us to understand the priority classes of these requests and implemented deadline-aware scheduling?
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Now, this framework is very powerful because it transfers to various stacks.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: You might be using vLLM or SGLang or TensorRT, but every technique fits into one of these quadrants.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So, whenever we think about any optimization to our model, we have to do a comparison and contrast with the previous techniques and see how all these stack with each other.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Now, whenever we think about scale, it's not just important to think about the performance of the model.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: We have to think about the cost economics as well.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: This is where
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: It's important to understand what metric we are trying to optimize because the cost is not just the cost of the GPU or the model.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: It is the cost of all these parameters, retries, storage, failures, network, and of course, the operational cost of development and all that stuff.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: What is important is to understand what is the key performance indicator for your product, which will add value to the users.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So, it's not important to optimize just cost per token or cost per request.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: We have to optimize cost per successful task because this is what actually users care about.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: And if we're able to optimize that, the cost for the overall product decreases and the users are much more happier.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Now let's talk about reliability, a little bit about reliability and what it means to prevent cascading failures.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Now the failure story is never a GPU is preempted or a GPU has died.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: The interesting story is the feedback loop that follows.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So a GPU can degrade, the latency can rise, the client retries, the queue depth increases, the healthy GPUs will saturate, which will follow more retries, more full regional failures.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: This is the classic cascading failures, but with a twist for agentic application, the KVCache.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: We cannot just casually restart or reroute to a different cluster.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: A cold pool has to warm up before it can absorb traffic, during which the hot pool has to take on all those requests.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: This is why it's important to design the loop breakers very deliberately.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: The circuit breakers at the routing layer, the admission control, which rejects rather than just queuing, the load shedding tied to queue depth, not just CPU or memory utilization.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: And we have to also think about retry budgets because if we don't think about all these things, the cost can scale much, much more quickly.
